key_terms.meaning: A set of objects or images that share a property, say ω₁ = handwritten '3', ω₂ = handwritten '8'.
The d numbers measured from one object, written x = (x₁, x₂, …, x_d)ᵀ, that the classifier works on.
The surface in feature space that separates one class region from another; a classifier is just a rule for placing it.
Assign x to class i whose mean vector mᵢ is nearest, using squared distance d² = (x − mᵢ)ᵀ(x − mᵢ).
Find the k labelled training vectors nearest to x and give x the majority label among them.
Assign x to the class i that maximises the posterior P(ωᵢ|x) ∝ p(x|ωᵢ)P(ωᵢ).
A layer of small learned kernels that slide over the input and produce a feature map per kernel.
The patch of the input image whose values can influence one unit of a given layer.
A shortcut that makes a block compute y = F(x) + x, so the block only has to learn the change from the input.
A candidate rectangle, a few hundred per image, that is likely to contain an object.
Cropping the feature map under a proposal and resizing it to a fixed grid so a fixed-size classifier can read it.
A predefined box of fixed size and shape attached to each grid cell, which the network adjusts into a real detection.
IoU = area of overlap ÷ area of union of two boxes; the usual test for whether a detection is correct.
Sort boxes by score, keep the best, and delete every remaining box whose IoU with it is above a threshold.
A network with only convolution and pooling layers, so its output is a spatial score map instead of one label.
A learnable upsampling layer that spreads each input value over a kernel-sized patch of the output.
One CNN reads RGB appearance frames, a second CNN reads stacked optical flow; the two scores are fused.
The per-pixel displacement field (u, v) that carries each point of one frame to the next.
A CNN encodes the image into a feature vector, and a recurrent decoder emits the caption one word at a time.
A generator G and a discriminator D trained against each other, D judging real versus fake images.
An encoder maps each image to a Gaussian in latent space and a decoder reconstructs from a sample, trained on the ELBO.

takeaways: Recognition is a decision in feature space: pick the class whose region the measured vector falls into.
Minimum distance needs only class means, k-NN needs all the training data, and Bayes needs class-conditional densities; they trade storage and assumption for accuracy.
A CNN replaces hand-designed features with kernels learned by backpropagation, so the same network works on faces and on circuit-board defects.
Depth helps only when gradients can flow; residual connections made very deep networks trainable and are the reason ResNet won ImageNet 2015.
Two-stage detectors (R-CNN family) propose then classify, which is accurate; single-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD) classify and regress boxes on a grid in one pass, which is fast.
Semantic segmentation is per-pixel classification: keep the feature map spatial, then upsample the coarse scores back to image size.
Video needs motion as well as appearance, so models read stacks of frames, optical flow, or 3D convolutions over time.
Captioning and visual QA join a vision encoder to a language decoder, turning a feature vector into a sequence of words.
GANs and VAEs learn the image distribution itself; inpainting is the same model run with the surviving pixels fixed as the condition.
bank_note: Long answers here are usually comparisons and pipeline diagrams: draw the block diagram, name the loss, state the speed/accuracy trade-off, and give numbers where you know them.

bank.q: Define pattern and pattern class. Explain the minimum distance classifier with a labelled training set, and state the assumption it makes about class shape.
outline: Define pattern as a description of an object, pattern class as a set sharing a property
Feature vector x of dimension d; each class has mean vector mᵢ
Decision rule: choose i minimising (x − mᵢ)ᵀ(x − mᵢ)
Expands to a linear discriminant when covariance is equal and isotropic
Assumption: classes are compact and roughly spherical around their means
Fails when classes overlap or have different spreads

bank.q: Explain the k-NN classifier. How is k chosen, what happens at k = 1 and at very large k, and how does the method compare with Bayes classification?
outline: Store all labelled samples; for a test x find k nearest by Euclidean distance
Majority vote among the k labels, ties broken by distance weighting
k = 1 gives jagged boundaries and is sensitive to noise
Large k smooths the boundary but blurs class edges; choose by cross-validation, use odd k for two classes
Bayes needs p(x|ωᵢ) and P(ωᵢ); k-NN needs no model but must keep the whole training set
k-NN error approaches twice the Bayes error as the data grows (cover–hart result)

bank.q: Describe the architecture of AlexNet and explain which design choices made it work on ImageNet.
outline: Five convolution layers, three fully connected layers, 1000-way softmax output
ReLU instead of sigmoid for faster training
Dropout in the fully connected layers
Data augmentation: crops, flips, colour jitter
Training on two GPUs, split across the feature maps
Local response normalisation and overlapping pooling as used in the paper
Won ImageNet 2012 with a large margin over hand-feature methods

bank.q: Explain VGG and ResNet. Why does simply stacking more layers make a plain network worse, and how does a residual block fix it?
outline: VGG: only 3×3 convolutions stacked, small kernels, depth 16 or 19, huge parameter count in the classifier
Plain deep networks show a degradation problem: training error itself rises with depth
Residual block: y = F(x) + x, identity shortcut, no new parameters
If the best layer is close to identity, F only has to learn a small residual, which is easier
Shortcuts give gradients a direct path to earlier layers, easing vanishing gradient
Bottleneck blocks and batch normalisation in practice
ResNet-152 won ImageNet 2015

bank.q: Explain R-CNN and Fast R-CNN. What was slow in R-CNN, and how did Fast R-CNN remove that cost?
outline: R-CNN: selective search gives ~2000 proposals, each warped and passed separately through a CNN, then an SVM classifies and a regressor corrects the box
Drawback: ~2000 forward passes per image, slow at test time, huge disk use for stored features
Fast R-CNN: run the CNN once on the whole image, then RoI-pool each proposal from the shared feature map
Multi-task loss: classification softmax plus bounding-box regression in one network
Training is end to end; remaining cost is the external selective-search proposal step

bank.q: Explain the YOLO detector: the output grid, what each cell predicts, the loss terms, and where it is weak.
outline: Divide the image into an S×S grid; each cell predicts B boxes with (x, y, w, h, confidence) plus class probabilities
Box coordinates are relative to the cell and predicted as square roots of width and height
Loss combines localisation error, confidence error for boxes containing and not containing objects, and classification error
One forward pass gives all detections, then NMS removes duplicates
Weak on small objects and on groups of close objects, because each cell is responsible for limited boxes

bank.q: Explain semantic segmentation with a fully convolutional network. Why must the classifier head be removed, and how are coarse scores brought back to full resolution?
outline: Segmentation labels every pixel with a class
Replace fully connected layers with 1×1 convolutions so the output stays a spatial map
Downsampling by pooling/stride reduces resolution by a factor of 32; the score map is coarse
Upsample with transposed convolution or bilinear interpolation to input size
Skip connections fuse fine detail from early layers with coarse semantics from late layers
Loss is per-pixel cross-entropy summed over the image

bank.q: Explain how action recognition is done in video. Describe the two-stream approach and 3D convolutional models.
outline: Video adds the time axis; a single frame often cannot tell an action from a pose
Two-stream: spatial stream on RGB frames for appearance, temporal stream on stacked optical flow for motion
Fuse the two softmax scores by averaging or SVM
3D convolution (for example C3D) extends the kernel to time, giving spatio-temporal feature maps
Cost: 3D convolution is memory heavy; long clips need sampling of frames

bank.q: Explain image captioning with a CNN–RNN encoder–decoder. Include the training loss and the role of attention.
outline: Encoder: a CNN turns the image into a feature vector, often the last spatial grid instead of one vector
Decoder: an LSTM or RNN emits one word per step, conditioned on the image feature and the previous words
Training maximises the log-likelihood of the reference caption, i.e. per-step cross-entropy
At test time words are fed back; greedy or beam search decoding
Attention lets the decoder weight different image regions at each word, improving long captions

bank.q: Explain how a GAN trains. Write the minimax objective, explain the roles of G and D, and describe mode collapse.
outline: Generator maps noise z to a fake image; discriminator outputs the probability that an image is real
Objective: min over G, max over D of E[log D(x)] + E[log(1 − D(G(z)))]
Alternate D and G updates; D learns to tell real from fake, G learns to fool D
At the optimum D = ½ and the loss equals the Jensen–Shannon divergence
Problems: unstable training, mode collapse where G produces a few samples, vanishing gradient if D is too strong

bank.q: A training set has three classes with mean vectors given. A test vector x is also given. Classify x by (a) minimum distance and (b) 3-NN using the listed sample points, and explain any disagreement between the two answers.
outline: Step 1 compute squared Euclidean distances (x − mᵢ)ᵀ(x − mᵢ) for each class mean
Step 2 pick the smallest; state the assigned class
Step 3 for 3-NN compute distances to individual samples, sort, take three smallest
Step 4 majority vote; report ties and how they are broken
Comment: disagreement arises when a class mean sits between clusters, i.e. the class is not compact, so the mean is a poor summary

bank.q: Given a network input of size 224×224×3, compute the output size of each layer for a stated sequence of convolution (3×3, stride 1, pad 1) and max-pool (2×2, stride 2) layers, then compute the total downsampling factor and the receptive field growth.
outline: Use out = floor((in + 2p − k)/s) + 1 for each layer
Pad 1 with 3×3 stride 1 keeps the spatial size unchanged
Each 2×2 stride-2 pooling halves width and height
After five such halvings the factor is 32, giving a 7×7 map
Receptive field grows by (k − 1) × (product of earlier strides) per layer

bank.q: Eight predicted boxes with scores and coordinates are given. Compute IoU with the ground-truth box for each, label each true or false positive at IoU ≥ 0.5, then apply non-maximum suppression and list the boxes that survive.
outline: IoU = intersection area ÷ union area; show both areas
Compare each IoU with the 0.5 threshold and mark TP or FP
Sort boxes by confidence descending
Keep the top box, delete every box with IoU > threshold against it
Repeat on the remaining boxes; report the kept list and the effect of the threshold on misses versus duplicates
Note the use of mAP over classes to summarise precision–recall

bank.q: Compare two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) with single-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD, RetinaNet) on accuracy, speed, small-object handling and training cost. Recommend one for (a) a phone app that reads number plates of moving cars and (b) counting cells in a microscope slide, with reasons.
outline: Two-stage: proposal step plus per-region classification; strong on small objects and localisation accuracy; slower
Single-stage: dense prediction over a grid with anchors; one forward pass; faster, weaker on small objects
RetinaNet's focal loss addresses the extreme foreground–background imbalance of single-stage training
Speed measured in frames per second at fixed input size; report as a trade-off, not an absolute number
Number plates: motion and phone hardware favour single-stage, quantised small model
Microscope cells: mostly one scale, but many small objects and no real-time need, favour two-stage or a segmentation model such as Mask R-CNN or U-Net

bank.q: A CNN classifier trained on clean X-ray images drops sharply in accuracy on images from another hospital. Analyse the likely causes and describe how you would diagnose and reduce the drop.
outline: Domain shift: different scanner, exposure, noise, patient population, class prevalence
Dataset bias: shortcut features such as text markers, borders, or scanner artefacts
Diagnose with confusion matrix per class, per-site accuracy, and feature visualisation
Remedies: intensity normalisation and histogram matching, augmentation, fine-tuning on a small target set, domain adaptation
Also check label noise, class imbalance, and calibration
Report sensitivity, specificity, AUC and confidence intervals; mention patient-level splitting to avoid leakage

bank.q: Compare GANs and VAEs for image generation and for inpainting. Which gives sharper images, which gives a usable likelihood, and how would you measure inpainting quality?
outline: VAE: encoder–decoder with a Gaussian latent, trained on reconstruction plus KL term; stable, blurred outputs, principled likelihood bound
GAN: no explicit likelihood, sharp samples, unstable training, mode collapse
Inpainting conditions on the visible pixels: mask-aware convolution or a loss that ignores the hole
Pixel losses alone give blur; adversarial loss sharpens, perception metrics change ranking
Metrics: PSNR and SSIM for fidelity, plus human or feature-distance judgement for realism
Evaluate with masked regions held out and report both metric families

glossary.def: Deciding which pattern class an observed feature vector belongs to.
A function gᵢ(x) per class such that x is assigned to the class with the largest value.
Distance scaled by the class covariance, d² = (x − m)ᵀΣ⁻¹(x − m), which removes correlation between features.
Fitting a model from inputs paired with known correct labels.
A layer turning K scores into probabilities that are positive and sum to one.
The training loss −Σ y log ŷ that punishes confident wrong predictions the most.
The chain rule applied layer by layer to get the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight.
The step, in pixels, by which a kernel moves across the input; stride 2 halves the output size.
Extra border pixels added around the input so kernel sliding does not shrink the map.
A fixed operation, usually max or average, over small windows that shrinks a feature map.
Normalising layer inputs by the mini-batch mean and variance, then scaling and shifting with learned parameters.
Starting from weights trained on a large dataset and fine-tuning them on a small target dataset.
The number a detector outputs for how likely a box is to contain an object of the predicted class.
The mean over classes of the area under the precision–recall curve at a stated IoU threshold.
A classical region-proposal method that merges similar neighbouring segments into candidate boxes.
Predicting at several resolutions of the same backbone so both small and large objects are found.
A loss that down-weights easy, numerous background examples so hard examples dominate training.
Increasing the spatial size of a feature map, by interpolation or by a transposed convolution.
Wiring a fine-resolution early feature map into a later layer to recover spatial detail.
Labelling every pixel of an image with a class, without separating individual instances.
Labelling pixels per object instance as well as per class, for example Mask R-CNN.
A recurrent unit with gates that carries information across many time steps without vanishing gradients.
The low-dimensional vector space in which a generative model represents images.
The failure of a GAN generator to cover the data distribution, producing only a few kinds of output.
